The recommended daily intake of chromium varies by age and gender: for children aged 1-3 years, it is 11 mcg/day; for those aged 4-8 years, it is 15 mcg/day; for females aged 9-13 years, it is 21 mcg/day, while for males in the same age group, it is 25 mcg/day. Females aged 14-18 years should consume 21 mcg/day. 2. Chromium picolinate and chromium histidinate have been granted orphan designation for the treatment of pediatric polycystic ovary syndrome in patients aged 16 years or younger. 3. Chromium can reduce the effectiveness of baloxavir marboxil by binding to cations in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to decreased absorption. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Animal studies in monkeys have shown that concurrent use of baloxavir with calcium, aluminum, or iron significantly reduces plasma levels. However, no human studies have been conducted. 4. Chromium and insulin degludec may enhance each other's effects through pharmacodynamic synergy, as both lower blood glucose levels. Caution and close monitoring are advised when using these together. 5. Chromium may similarly interact with other forms of insulin, including insulin aspart, insulin inhaled, insulin detemir, insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, insulin lispro, insulin NPH, and regular human insulin, by increasing their effects through pharmacodynamic synergy. Close monitoring is recommended in all cases. 6. Chromium can increase the effects of oral antidiabetic medications such as glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide, metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, and vildagliptin through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown, but caution is advised. 7. Certain corticosteroids, including cortisone, deflazacort, dexamethasone, fludrocortisone, hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone, prednisolone, prednisone, and triamcinolone, can decrease chromium levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 8. Aluminum hydroxide, calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and sodium citrate/citric acid can reduce chromium levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. To minimize the interaction, doses should be separated by at least 2 hours. 9. Aspirin (oral, rectal, or in combination with citric acid and sodium bicarbonate) may increase chromium levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 10. Budesonide may decrease chromium levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 11. Indomethacin may increase chromium levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 12. Rose hips may enhance chromium levels by improving gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 13. Chromium can decrease the levels or effects of omadacycline and sarecycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Multivalent cation-containing products may impair the absorption of tetracyclines, reducing their efficacy. Doses of tetracyclines should be separated from these products. 14. Direct intravenous or intramuscular administration of undiluted chromium solutions, such as chromic chloride injection (4 mcg/mL), is contraindicated due to the acidic pH, which can cause significant tissue irritation. 15. In patients with severe kidney disease, it may be necessary to reduce or omit chromium and zinc doses, as these elements are primarily eliminated through the urine. 16. This product contains aluminum, which can be toxic. Prolonged parenteral administration in patients with impaired kidney function, including premature neonates, may lead to toxic aluminum levels. Premature neonates are particularly at risk due to immature kidneys and the need for large amounts of calcium and phosphate solutions, which also contain aluminum. Research indicates that aluminum accumulation at levels greater than 4-5 mcg/kg/day is associated with central nervous system and bone toxicity. Tissue loading may occur even at lower administration rates. 17. Chromium solutions should only be used if they are clear and the seal is intact. Chromic chloride injection (4 mcg/mL) must be prepared using a pharmacy-directed admixture program with aseptic techniques in a laminar flow environment. The solution should be used promptly in a single operation without repeated penetrations. Any unused portion should be discarded immediately after the admixture procedure is completed, as the solution contains no preservatives. 18. When assessing the contribution of chromium supplements to glucose homeostasis, it is important to consider the possibility that the patient may have diabetes. 19. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with chromic chloride. It is unknown whether chromic chloride can cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant women or affect reproductive capacity. Chromic chloride should only be given to pregnant women if clearly indicated. 20. It is not known whether this drug is excreted in human milk. As many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised when administering chromic chloride injection (4 mcg/mL) to nursing women. 21. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk, making this drug generally acceptable for use during pregnancy.
